analysis.one_liner: Lets federal watchdogs investigate asbestos bankruptcy trusts and opens claimant records to companies fighting asbestos lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill went to the Senate Judiciary Committee in March 2018 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company facing asbestos lawsuits goes bankrupt, a court creates a trust to pay people who were exposed to asbestos. This bill would give the Justice Department's bankruptcy watchdog new power to investigate those trusts, audit the claims they pay, and prosecute people who file fraudulent claims. It would also require trusts to hand over information about who is being paid to anyone involved in an asbestos lawsuit, and would require trusts to report claimants who are on Medicare to the federal government.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and insurers still fighting asbestos lawsuits in court. They would gain access to trust claimant records, which they can use to challenge or discount the claims of people suing them, and new audits and investigations would slow the payout of trust money.

how_it_helps.text: Gives the U.S. Trustee Program, the Justice Department's bankruptcy oversight office, statutory authority to investigate the administration and operation of asbestos bankruptcy trusts, including trusts created before the bill's enactment [S2][S3].

Authorizes the U.S. Trustee to conduct discovery, audit any claim paid or to be paid by a trust, refer suspected false claims to U.S. attorneys for prosecution, and ask courts to impose remedies for misuse of trust funds [S3].
Creates new federal crimes for knowingly making a false representation to, or a false claim against, an asbestos bankruptcy trust [S2][S3].
Requires trusts to provide information about payments and demands for payment to parties in asbestos-related lawsuits, with the trust able to charge the requester for reasonable costs [S3].
Requires trust administrators to determine within 60 days whether a claimant is entitled to Medicare and to report that information to the Secretary of Health and Human Services [S3].
Replaces the court-appointed legal representative for future asbestos claimants with a representative appointed by the U.S. Trustee and approved by the court [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: People sickened by asbestos exposure who rely on the trusts for compensation. Their claims would face audits and investigations, their claim information would be shared with companies suing or being sued over asbestos, and the new review process would add delay to payments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Asbestos victims claiming from bankruptcy trusts

drawbacks.text: The bill requires trusts to turn over claimant payment information to parties in asbestos lawsuits [S3]. Those parties are typically the solvent companies and insurers defending victims' suits, so the same data used to audit fraud would also help them contest, discount, or settle claims for less.

Moving the appointment of the future claims representative from the court to the U.S. Trustee, a Justice Department office, takes that role away from the judge overseeing the bankruptcy and hands it to an executive agency [S3].

Audits, investigations, and the Medicare reporting requirement add administrative steps to every claim [S3]. For claimants who are elderly and seriously ill, each added step can mean a longer wait for money they were already awarded a right to under the bankruptcy plan.
The bill extends the U.S. Trustee's authority specifically to cases in Alabama and North Carolina, districts that otherwise operate under a different bankruptcy-administration system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Targeting fraudulent claims has real value: money taken from a trust by a false claim is money an actual victim never receives. But the bill's main operating tools, discovery into claimant files, information-sharing with litigation adversaries, and audit authority, weigh far more heavily on legitimate claimants and their lawyers than on the fraud it targets, and the information-sharing provision reads as a benefit to the companies defending asbestos suits. A narrower anti-fraud bill without the litigation-discovery provisions would have been easier to defend.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on March 15, 2018, read twice, and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it stayed until the 115th Congress ended without any hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Thom Tillis, joined by Sens. John Cornyn and Chuck Grassley, introduced the bill on March 15, 2018 [S3][S1].
Five Republican senators cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did [S4].
The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary on the day it was introduced [S5][S1].
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 115th Congress on January 3, 2019 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Asbestos victims and their lawyers kept the existing trust system unchanged, since no new disclosure, audit, or investigative requirements were enacted. Solvent asbestos defendants and insurers did not get the access to trust claimant data they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Asbestos victims, whose claims stayed unchanged

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor, both co-introducers, and all five cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on; the bill died in a committee run by one of its own co-introducers.

industries.note: The bill would give them access to trust claimant records for use in their own lawsuits against asbestos victims, plus audits that slow the payout of trust money. Every dollar they save in litigation or delay comes at the cost of compensation to sick claimants.

industries.industry: Asbestos bankruptcy trusts and the asbestos plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: Trusts would face new audits, investigation authority, criminal exposure for false claims, Medicare reporting duties, and mandatory information-sharing with litigation parties. Their interest in keeping the current system is aligned with victims' interest in being paid promptly, though the anti-fraud provisions also protect trust assets that belong to victims.

Trusts would have to report Medicare-entitled claimants to HHS within 60 days, letting Medicare recover payments from trust settlements it otherwise might miss. This is cost-shifting between funds, not new money for victims.
